We examined EEG signal strength using time-resolved global field power (GFP), spatial configuration using topographic analysis of variance (TANOVA), and task-specific neural differentiation using the global dissimilarity index (DISS). We also examined the relationship between neural and behavioral measures, including digit-span scores and speech onset time. We found that speaking was associated with higher GFP than silent reading in the 388–800 ms interval, with no significant effects of group or group × task interaction, indicating similar EEG strength across groups. TANOVA revealed age-related differences in scalp topography in the 229–334 ms and 377–538 ms intervals, a task effect in the 618–723 ms interval, and a group × task interaction in the 562–636 ms interval. Notably, young adults had greater DISS than older adults during the 508–629 ms and 660–800 ms intervals, reflecting more distinct neural configurations for speaking and reading. We did not find significant correlations between DISS or GFP and behavioral measures, and the two groups performed similarly on behavioral measures. Overall, aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between speaking and silent reading, especially during later processing stages (e.g., motor command preparation), while preserving overall EEG activity and behavioral performance. These findings may suggest that aging reduces neural network specificity (as previously suggested) and alters spatial organization without necessarily impairing behavior.

item.title: Sublexical compensatory reorganization of Chinese character recognition in Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
Journal of clinical and experimental neuropsychology
Objective This study investigated the cognitive-functional shift in visual character recognition across the cognitive decline trajectory, ranging from healthy aging through Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) to Mild Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Specifically, it was hypothesized that as global semantic networks degrade, the reliance on rapid holistic processing decreases, prompting a compensatory shift toward sublexical features. Method Using a controlled unmasked priming lexical decision paradigm, this study evaluated behavioral performance across three distinct participant groups (N = 30 per group): healthy controls (HC), individuals with MCI, and patients with Mild AD. The experimental stimuli consisted of 80 Chinese phonograms matched across key psycholinguistic properties. This study utilized mixed-design Analyses of Variance (ANOVAs) alongside item-level hierarchical multiple regression (HMR) models to isolate the specific drivers of reaction times, assessing the predictive power of visual complexity, whole-character frequency, semantic transparency, and phonetic regularity. Results The analytical models revealed distinctly divergent psycholinguistic trajectories. The HC group demonstrated highly efficient holistic processing, with performance primarily driven by whole-character frequency. Conversely, the MCI group exhibited a unique transitional cognitive profile, characterized by a simultaneous reliance on both holistic whole-word access and analytic sublexical features. Crucially, in the Mild AD tgroup, the holistic processing advantage was entirely abolished. This functional disintegration triggered a compensatory reorganization toward bottom-up sublexical properties, with patients relying heavily on semantic transparency and phonetic regularity to achieve semantic access. Conclusions These findings demonstrate a linguistic Compensation-Related Utilization of Neural Circuits Hypothesis (CRUNCH) effect within the degenerating brain. As top-down lexical-semantic hubs deteriorate, reflected behaviorally in this paradigm by the loss of holistic processing advantages, the cognitive system actively compensates by upregulating bottom-up, sublexical pathways. Furthermore, the transitional sublexical dependency observed during the MCI stage highlights the translational potential of psycholinguistic variables as sensitive, noninvasive behavioral biomarkers for the early screening and monitoring of dementia.

item.title: Intratumoral and Peritumoral Functional Connectivity Reveals Network-Level Signatures of Glioma.
item.description:
MedComm
Gliomas are recognized as network-level diseases that remodel functional connectivity across the brain. Using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data from 306 patients with pathologically confirmed glioma at two hospitals, we delineated individualized intra- and peritumoral functional networks to quantify tumor-related alterations. Two novel indices-the ratio of intratumoral functional regions (RIFR) and ratio of peritumoral tumor-related regions (RPTR)-were proposed to describe network remodeling. Both indices were related to pathological, structural, functional, cognitive, language, and survival measures. Lower RIFR indicated diminished intratumoral connectivity and worse prognosis, while higher values reflected preserved network integration and longer survival. Models incorporating network features yielded areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.90 in training and 0.86-0.88 in external validation. Supporting analyses suggested that intratumoral functional regions are associated with distinct molecular and cellular characteristics. These findings suggest that intra- and peritumoral networks reflect biologically and functionally distinct tumor subregions and are associated with network-level alterations, brain function, and patient outcome. Interpretation is limited by the hemodynamic basis of rs-fMRI, incomplete data, and limited intraoperative validation. These findings identify individualized intra- and peritumoral connectivity measures as candidate markers of glioma-associated network remodeling and prognosis that require prospective, multimodal validation.

item.title: Multimodal modeling of the ictal onset zone in refractory insular epilepsy and seizure outcome of magnetic resonance-guided laser interstitial therapy: A pediatric single-center retrospective study.
item.description:
Epilepsia
Objective This study was undertaken to evaluate seizure outcomes after magnetic resonance-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (MRgLITT) in children with insular epilepsy and to assess how the extent of ablation overlaps with multimodal definitions of the ictal onset zone (IOZ). Methods We conducted a retrospective, single-center study including consecutive pediatric patients treated with MRgLITT for insular epilepsy. All patients underwent presurgical evaluation including electroencephalography (EEG) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI); fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) and stereo-EEG (SEEG) were performed in negative-MRI cases. Epileptic zone was identified by visual analysis of SEEG recording. Postablation contrast-enhancing volumes were manually segmented and coregistered with IOZ estimates derived from Multi-centre Epilepsy Lesion Detection (MELD) MRI analysis, FDG-PET voxel-based analysis, and the Epileptogenicity Index, when available. Spatial concordance between modalities was assessed using Dice similarity coefficients, and the proportion of each IOZ modality encompassed within the ablation volume was correlated with postoperative seizure outcomes (International League Against Epilepsy classification). Results Eight children (median age = 10.4 years, range = 2.3-17) were included, with a median postoperative follow-up of 38 months. Two patients had insular tumors, and both achieved seizure freedom after complete ablation. Among the six MRI-negative patients, FDG-PET revealed insular hypometabolism in four, MELD detected a median of one insular cluster (range 1-3), and SEEG identified focal insular ictal activity in three cases. Overall, four negative-MRI patients achieved seizure freedom: three after MRgLITT alone and one after MRgLITT combined with frontal opercular resection. One transient postoperative aphasia was observed. Intermodality spatial concordance was low across all comparisons. A greater proportion of FDG-PET hypometabolism included in the ablation volume was associated with better seizure outcomes (p = .012). Significance MRgLITT is an effective and safe treatment option for focal insular epilepsy in children, either as standalone therapy or in a combined approach. Optimal outcome depends on accurate preoperative delineation of the IOZ and its complete ablation.

item.title: Prior visual context accelerates the emergence of object representations
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Our knowledge about how the world is structured allows for predictions about what objects we might see next. Visual context is known to impact the perception of subsequent objects, but we don’t know what context does to the mental representation of those objects. Using MEG, we tested how a scene context changes the neural representation of visual objects, and whether the context simply enhances expected object representations, or if it acts to reorganise the temporal trajectory of object information in the brain. Using temporal generalisation decoding, we show that multiple dimensions of semantic information are shifted up to 200 ms earlier when the object and the prior context are congruent, and this temporally-shifted decoding was related to behavioural object recognition speed. This suggests that prior context can warp the temporal trajectory through which object representations are accessed and accelerate the emergence of semantic object representations in the mind.

item.title: Evolutionary dynamics of maximal syllable complexity show no universal bias rooted in jaw biomechanics
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Linguistic evolution has given rise to variation in the degree of syllable complexity that any given language permits. However, several models of language converge in predicting a universal bias towards the consonant-vowel (CV) structure (or a broader strong-weak asymmetry). This is closely tied to incremental speech processing, and in evolutionary terms has been linked to certain rhythmic orofacial displays in non-human primates. Yet, whether linguistic evolution really reflects such a universal tendency is an open question, one that we aim to address using phylogenetic comparative methods. Modeling change according to a continuous-time Markov process, we estimate transition rates for maximal onset and coda sizes (i.e. grammatical rules) across 5 language families. We demonstrate that a lineage-specific model outperforms a global model, and further explore the nature of lineage-specific long-term preferences and rates of change on multiple levels. We show that the former drive inter-family variation more than the latter. Generally, particulars turn out to impact syllable complexity more than any universal biomechanically or neurocognitively motivated biases do, implying that evolutionary continuity with our primate ancestors may have been overstated for this domain of language.

item.title: Perceived social value is more strongly linked to gossip decisions with age in adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Gossip is central to social exchange, yet how adolescents select what to share and with whom remains unclear. Across two endent samples aged 10–18 years (behavioural, n = 98; fMRI, n = 101 scanned), adolescents read information about absent third parties, chose whether and with whom to share it, and rated interest, usefulness and emotional response. Sharing frequency showed no detectable age association. The association between interest ratings and sharing strengthened with age in both samples; usefulness showed a smaller age interaction. Adolescents selected close friends more often with age when sharing. During scenario reading, before participants reported choices, BOLD responses in a left inferior frontal cluster tracked subsequent interest ratings more strongly with age (n = 92), also within regions defined by a mental-state judgment localizer. Together, these findings link age in adolescence to stronger valuation-to-decision coupling for interest and a greater proportion of sharing directed to close friends.

item.title: CortexDecoder: fMRI-to-image Reconstruction from Cortical Flatmaps
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Recent advances in brain decoding work has shown the potential of Vision Transformers (ViTs) to learn mappings from neural representation to visual features. Here we present CortexDecoder, a brain decoding framework mapping fMRI flatmaps to images viewed by subjects. Flatmaps are neural responses projected onto cortical surfaces and then unfolded into 2D images. We demonstrate that (1) flatmaps preserve sufficient signal to achieve high performance in brain decoding; raw fMRI data has noisy signals and high-dimensionality which makes decoding a difficult task. (2) Reshaping raw fMRI data into flatmaps allows for clean patch-based tokenization. This allows us to harness state-of-the-art Vision Transformers to learn meaningful neural representations and preserve spatial encoding. To do this, we pass flatmap patches into a pretrained CortexMAE encoder to obtain brain tokens. A lightweight cross-attention bridge then learns to map these brain tokens to image features. Our cross-attention bridge is split into two modules; the semantic module for predicting CLIP embeddings and the lower-level module to generate low-level image reconstruction. Finally, a fine-tuned SDXL (Stable Diffusion XL) takes this low-level reconstruction image as the initial image. Conditioned by the CLIP semantic embedding, the SDXL produces the final reconstruction image. In single-subject evaluations, CortexDecoder achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art brain decoding methods, demonstrating the effectiveness of flatmap based neural representations for visual reconstruction. All code will be available at https://github.com/teooi/CortexDecoder .

item.title: Metastasis Extraction From Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer Clinical Notes Using Large Language Model-Based Classification: Retrospective Comparative Study.
item.description:
JMIR cancer
Background Identification of metastasis status in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is a critical part of understanding disease prognosis, treatment courses, trial eligibility, and population-level cancer surveillance. However, metastasis status is inconsistently recorded in structured cancer registry fields, since manual abstraction of clinical notes is often an error-prone process. This challenge highlights an opportunity for leveraging large language models (LLMs) to conduct high-scale metastasis extraction from real-world clinical documentation. Objective We conducted a retrospective, multicohort comparative evaluation of 3 distinct LLMs for 2 independent classification tasks: overall metastasis presence at any site and brain/central nervous system (CNS) metastasis presence. We evaluated model performance on 2 independent NSCLC cohorts: one with registry labels and another with manual annotations. We further explored whether our methods could analyze clinical documentation and recover missing information in structured registry fields. Methods Patient cohorts were derived from the Winship Cancer Institute. Cohort 1 (n=579 patients; 24,887 notes across 69 note types; 2023-2025) used registry-linked metastasis fields as the reference standard. Cohort 2 (n=22 patients; 644 radiology notes; 2010-2021) was drawn from 2 completed randomized trials and used dual-annotated labels (Cohen κ: 0.93 overall metastasis; 0.88 CNS metastasis) as the reference standard. We fine-tuned the GatorTron-base encoder model for each independent binary classification task. We evaluated MedGemma-27B-text and Llama 3.1-70B using zero-shot prompting. A separate cohort of 675 patients with missing registry labels was used for an exploratory missingness-recovery analysis, validated against annotations of a random subsample. Our best-performing model was used to conduct further site-specific metastasis classification, based on available registry data. Results More than half (675/1260, 54%) of initially identified cohort 1 patients had missing or unknown registry metastasis labels. MedGemma demonstrated the best performance in overall metastasis classification (cohort 1: F1 -score=0.80; cohort 2 patient-level: F1 -score=1.0; cohort 2 note-level: F1 -score=0.93). For brain/CNS metastasis, Llama3 performed best in both cohorts (cohort 1: F1 -score=0.79; cohort 2 patient-level: F1 -score=0.93; cohort 2 note-level: F1 -score=0.86). The fine-tuned GatorTron model showed strong performance for classification of overall metastasis in cohort 1 (F1 -score=0.72). Error analysis indicated that several model errors reflected incomplete registry labels, ambiguous clinical language, or missing documentation. In the exploratory recovery analysis, model predictions agreed with manual annotations at an accuracy of 0.90 and F1 -score of 0.89. Additional site-specific metastasis classification by MedGemma demonstrated high performance for liver metastasis (F1 -score=0.82) and bone metastasis (F1 -score=0.79). Conclusions All models demonstrated relatively high performance. The zero-shot generative models were more robust to nuanced documentation and context-dependent brain/CNS metastasis extraction. The fine-tuned encoder model demonstrated strong classification performance but may have been limited by potential inaccuracies in the registry reference standards during model training. This study further demonstrated the potential of LLMs in recovering plausible structured labels from narrative text, complementing cancer registries for metastasis ascertainment.

item.title: Midlife and Late-Life Alzheimer Disease Blood Biomarkers and 11-Year Cognitive Decline.
item.description:
Neurology
Background and objectives Plasma biomarkers of Alzheimer disease (AD) neuropathology (amyloid-β42 to amyloid β40 [Aβ42/40] ratio, phosphorylated tau at threonine [p-tau181]), neurodegeneration (neurofilament light [NfL]), and neuroinflammation (glial fibrillary acidic protein [GFAP]) in late-life are associated with cognitive decline. Whether these biomarkers in midlife are predictive of subsequent cognitive decline, and whether they are associated with different cognitive domains, is uncertain. In this study, we investigated associations of midlife and late-life plasma Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP with late-life change in domain-specific (memory, language, and executive function) and global cognitive function. Methods We performed a prospective cohort analysis of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Neurocognitive Study (ARIC-NCS). Outcome follow-up was from ARIC visit 5 (2011-2013) to visit 9 (2021-2022). We included all individuals from ARIC field centers (Jackson, Mississippi; Forsyth County, North Carolina; Washington County, Maryland; and Minneapolis suburbs, Minnesota) with biomarkers measured from stored specimens in midlife (visit 3, 1993-1995, mean age 59.0 years) and late-life (visit 5, 2011-2013, mean age 76.8 years). Aβ42/40, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were measured with the Quanterix Simoa platform and standardized to visit 3 to facilitate cross-biomarker comparisons of their rate of change from midlife to late-life. We estimated change in memory, language, executive function, and global cognition factor scores from visit 5 to visit 9 with linear mixed-effect models. Results In 1,515 included participants, 60.7% (n = 920) were female and 25.5% (n = 387) were Black. Each SD increase in p-tau181 in midlife was significantly associated with faster late-life memory decline (β = -0.030 [95% CI -0.059 to -0.001] SD. Midlife Aβ42/40, NfL, and GFAP were not associated with subsequent decline in any cognitive domain. In late-life, p-tau181, NfL, and GFAP were significantly associated with faster decline in different cognitive domains, with the strongest associations seen with memory (β = -0.091 [95% CI -0.123 to -0.058] SD; β = -0.064 [95% CI -0.106 to -0.023] SD; and β = -0.048 [95% CI -0.082 to -0.013] SD, respectively). Discussion Midlife p-tau181 was associated with faster 11-year memory decline beginning 20 years later in the ARIC cohort, which underscores a potentially long prodromal phase of cognitive decline that could precede dementia onset. In late-life, biomarkers for AD, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation were associated with faster decline across different cognitive domains, but associations remained strongest for p-tau181 and memory.

item.title: Bridging language phenotypes, neural dynamics and gene regulation in autism.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs) affect approximately 1% of the global population, with prevalence rising over recent decades. Although ASDs are heritable (~70%), translating genetic findings into effective therapeutics remains challenging due to the vast number of implicated risk genes (>700) and the limited influence of individual genes on disease expression. Their collective impact and convergent expression patterns of small-effect genes provide insights into ASD-related neurobiological mechanisms. Current interventions remain symptom-focused and do not address underlying neurodevelopmental mechanisms. Emerging approaches in functional genomics offer new insights into ASD pathogenesis by exploring gene expression diversity, yet clinical applications remain distant. Language deficits are among the most frequent and disabling features of ASD, profoundly affecting individuals' and families' quality of life. Recent evidence from neuroimaging and electrophysiology studies suggests disrupted neural oscillatory dynamics are linked to language deficits in ASD. Several ASD-associated genes have been implicated in biological pathways involved in the regulation of brain oscillatory dynamics, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between genetic variation, altered brain rhythms, and language impairment. We propose a neurophysiological imaging genetics framework that leverages neural oscillatory profiles as endophenotypes for targeted investigation and as functional readouts of gene expression. Within this framework, neuromodulation is proposed as an experimental approach to investigate and potentially modulate altered oscillatory dynamics associated with speech communication deficits in ASD, while integrating oscillation-related ASD candidate genes into a symptom-oriented model of functional genomics. This approach shows how integrating genetic variation, non-invasive neuroimaging, and behavioral phenotypes can advance our understanding of ASD and inform targeted, mechanism-based interventions.

item.title: Multiscale neural signatures of long-lag repetition learning: a simultaneous fNIRS-EEG study.
item.description:
Neurophotonics
Significance Repetition-based learning supports word recognition and reading fluency, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly where deficits in consolidating repeated linguistic input may underlie reading and language difficulties. Establishing reliable neural markers of repetition-based learning is a critical first step toward characterizing the phenotypes of these difficulties in children. Aim We developed a whole-brain simultaneous functional near-infrared spectroscopy-electroencephalography (fNIRS-EEG) approach to capture fast temporal electrophysiological and spatially accurate hemodynamic signals during long-lag repetition learning. Approach Thirty participants performed a semantic judgment task with words repeated across four runs with intervening items, modeling repetition demands central to reading instruction. A multimodal decoding framework integrating electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and cross-modal fNIRS-EEG correlation features was used to classify repetition-based learning. Results Repeated words showed response time reductions. EEG captured a frontal N400-range repetition-related negativity and attenuation of alpha-beta suppression, reflecting changes in recognition-related and post-recognition processing. fNIRS revealed left inferior frontal and superior temporal efficiency increases alongside right supramarginal activation, suggesting integrative processing. Multimodal classifiers outperformed unimodal classifiers, indicating that each modality captured complementary aspects of learning. Conclusions Combining fNIRS and EEG with multimodal machine learning provides a richer characterization of repetition-based learning than either modality alone, establishing a framework for phenotyping language learning capacity and identifying neural markers of reading difficulties in pediatric populations.
